November 18, 2026

What Should a University Degree Prove After AI?

As AI makes routine academic work easier to reproduce, universities must demonstrate that their graduates can do more than produce known answers.

Universities have a problem.

For a long time, they offered two promises at once. The first was access to knowledge. The second was access to better work. If someone wanted to become an engineer, a lawyer, a physician, or enter any number of professional careers, the university was the place where the necessary knowledge could be found and where society certified that it had been acquired.

The two promises reinforced each other. Knowledge was difficult to obtain, and those who possessed it were scarce. A degree therefore gave access not only to a profession, but also to a better economic position.

That arrangement was never universal. University required opportunity, preparation, discipline, and a certain kind of academic ability. Not everyone could enter, and not everyone who entered could finish. Fairly or not, the degree became a signal: the person holding it was assumed to know things that most people did not and to be capable of work that most people could not do.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to weaken that signal.

A surprising amount of practical knowledge is now accessible through models. Anyone can request an explanation of a legal concept, help with a program, a statistical analysis, or a description of a medical process and receive a useful answer in seconds.

This does not mean that receiving an answer is the same as understanding it. Someone with deep training will normally ask better questions, recognize mistakes, and understand what a model leaves out. Established knowledge and the effort required to learn it remain necessary.

The problem is what conventional academic work now proves. If a model can solve the standard exercises and produce an acceptable version of the final assignment, completing those tasks no longer demonstrates the same capabilities it once did. AI does not erase the value of education. It weakens the evidentiary value of a degree built mainly around recalling information and reproducing known answers.

In one limited sense, the undergraduate degree may be following the path of the high school diploma.

The analogy is not that AI will cause everyone to attend university. It is that what once counted as advanced preparation can gradually become an expected foundation. In the United States, the proportion of 18-year-olds receiving a high school diploma rose from about 9 percent in 1910 to more than half in 1940 (Goldin & Katz, 1997). University education later experienced its own version of this transition as employers began demanding bachelor's degrees for jobs that had not previously required them (Fuller & Raman, 2017).

AI adds a different kind of pressure. It makes established knowledge and routine intellectual work easier to access and reproduce. The degree may therefore remain useful—even necessary—without remaining distinctive. If that happens, universities will need to demonstrate something beyond mastery of established material: the capacity to formulate a problem, evaluate evidence, and work where no answer has been specified in advance.

If established knowledge becomes foundational rather than distinctive, the next question is where intellectual value moves. The distinction between reproducing a procedure and directing intellectual work is not new. In de Prony's production of logarithmic and trigonometric tables, mathematicians designed the methods while human “computers”—famously, though perhaps apocryphally, described as unemployed hairdressers—performed the routine arithmetic (Grattan-Guinness, 1990; Roegel, 2010). Leibniz made the same distinction when he wrote that “it is unworthy of excellent men to lose hours like slaves in the labor of calculation” (Leibniz, 1685/1929, p. 181).

AI extends that old division beyond arithmetic. As more routine execution can be delegated, value moves toward choosing the problem, designing the method, evaluating the evidence, and taking responsibility for the result. Those are the capabilities a university degree must increasingly prove.

Universities should not stop teaching established knowledge. Without a foundation, students cannot judge a model's answer or investigate a new question. But transmitting that knowledge can no longer be the distinctive endpoint of higher education. It must be the preparation for work in which the answer is not already available.

The degree may therefore have to move in two directions at once: its taught component becomes more like high school—a necessary foundation—while its culminating work becomes more like research.

The bachelor's thesis is an obvious place to begin.

A thesis should provide evidence of what the student can do, not merely of what they can submit. That requires a supervised process in which the student formulates the problem, explains the decisions, confronts evidence, and defends the result. The use of AI is not itself the problem. The problem is work in which the student's intellectual contribution can no longer be identified.

This does not mean that every undergraduate must produce a scientific revolution. A serious thesis might study an unexplored local problem, produce new evidence, run an experiment, construct and evaluate a real system, or combine ideas in a way for which there is no predetermined answer. The result need not be new to humanity, but the inquiry must be authentic and the judgment must belong to the student.

The goal is not to demand more pages or make degrees artificially harder. It is to change what difficulty means. Reproducing established answers is becoming cheap. Choosing a meaningful problem, confronting reality, and determining whether an answer deserves to be trusted remain difficult.

In this limited sense, the bachelor's degree may have to move closer to the PhD. Not in duration, specialization, or the expectation of a major scientific contribution, but in spirit: students should spend at least some time working where no answer has been specified in advance.

Universities do not have to compete with AI at producing explanations of what humanity already knows. They must teach the foundations and then test what comes after: deciding which questions matter, recognizing plausible but mistaken answers, and accepting responsibility for a conclusion.

After AI, a degree should not merely certify that its holder can produce an answer. It should show that they can act when there is no settled answer—and when an answer generated by a model is not enough.
